inline.s: The holy host of the three quarters, in reverence, return as one.
In the realm of sands their light of discourse shines.
They dwell in deep samādhi's joy, with the mind of the four fearlessnesses.
Each brings wondrous flowers of every kind, and famous incenses all delightful.
Together they play celestial music, a hundred thousand harmonious and elegant notes.
To offer to the Teacher of Devas and Humans, whose fame is heard throughout the ten directions.
Perfect in the power of awe-inspiring spirit, well learned in every Dharma gate.
Among all manner of offerings, they cultivate diligently without weariness or slackness.
The radiance of merit and wisdom can shatter every darkness.
All with reverent minds present every precious and wondrous offering.
They behold that peerless land, and the host of bodhisattvas without bound.
May we swiftly attain bodhi, and a pure realm like that of Peace and Bliss.
The World-Honored One knows their joy of desire, vast and inconceivable.
He smiles and reveals his golden countenance: it shall be accomplished as you have wished.
Knowing all dharmas to be illusory, and Buddha-lands as a dream or an echo.
Ever vowing to adorn, they shall accomplish a subtle and wondrous land.
By the power of their vows, bodhisattvas cultivate the supreme course of bodhi.
Knowing the land to be like an image or shadow, they bring forth the mind of vast vows.
If one seeks the all-pure, peerless, boundless Buddha-land,
let him hear the holy name of the Buddha, and vow to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
If there be bodhisattvas whose aspiration seeks a pure land,
let them know the selflessness of dharmas, and vow to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss.

Again, Ananda, all the bodhisattvas in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are settled in utmost bodhi, and are one life from Buddhahood. The only exceptions are those great beings of the resolve who can roar the lion's roar and don the great armor, who for the deliverance of the host of beings cultivate the great nirvana.

Again, Ananda, the hearers in that Buddha-land all have light of body that can illumine one fathom. The light of the bodhisattvas shines as far as a hundred thousand fathoms, save for the radiance of two bodhisattvas, which forever illumines a billion worlds.”
Ananda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, what are the names of those two bodhisattvas?”

The Buddha told Ananda: “Listen well now. Those two bodhisattvas: the first is named Avalokiteśvara, the second is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. Ananda, these two bodhisattvas, having relinquished the measure of their lives in the Sahā world, are born in that land. Ananda, the bodhisattvas born in that Land of Ultimate Bliss all possess the thirty-two marks; their skin and flesh are soft, their faculties keen and sharp, their wisdom and skillful means such that there is no differentiated dharma they do not fully know. In meditative concentration and spiritual penetration they sport with ease; none of them are of thin merit or dull faculties. Among those bodhisattvas, those who attain the first patience, or the second, are immeasurable and boundless, and some have realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. Ananda, the bodhisattvas of that land, until they attain bodhi, never fall into the evil destinies. In whatever life they are born, they can know their past lives. The only exception is those who appear in the world within lands of the five turbidities. Ananda, the bodhisattvas of that land, every morning, make offerings to the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas in other directions. Whatever they may wish for — all kinds of flower garlands, perfumed ointments, powdered incense, banners and streamers, silk canopies, and all manner of music — by the Buddha's spiritual power all appears in their hands, and they make offering to those Buddhas. Such offerings are vast and abundant, countless and boundless, inconceivable. Or again, if they delight to seek all kinds of famous flowers, flowers of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of lights and colors, all appear in their hands, and they scatter them in offering to the Buddhas. Ananda, the flowers they scatter at once become flower canopies in the sky. The smallest of those canopies fills ten yojanas. If they do not again scatter fresh flowers upon them, the flowers already scattered never fall. Ananda, some flower canopies fill twenty yojanas, and likewise thirty or forty, even a thousand yojanas; or they equal four continents, or cover a small chiliocosm, a middle chiliocosm, even a billion worlds. These bodhisattvas give rise to a rare thought and attain great joy. In the morning hour they serve, make offering to, revere, and praise immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas, and having planted all roots of goodness, in that same morning hour they return to their own land. All this comes from the original vows and added majesty of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and from the fact that they once made offering to the Tathāgatas, and their roots of goodness continue without deficiency, because they have cultivated them well, gathered them well, and perfected them well.

Again, Ananda, the words spoken by the host of bodhisattvas in that Land of Ultimate Bliss accord with omniscience. In all that they make use of, they grasp at nothing. Wandering throughout Buddha-lands, they have neither love nor weariness, and no craving. They have no thought of craving, no thought of self, no thought of affliction, no thought of I, no thought of quarreling, opposition, resentment, or anger. Why is this? Because those bodhisattvas have, toward all beings, a mind of great compassion and benefit, a mind soft and without obstruction, a mind undefiled, a mind without resentment or hate, a mind equal, tamed, and still, a mind of patience, a mind of patience and taming, a mind of even and clear concentration without distraction, a mind without covering, a pure mind, a most pure mind, a shining mind, a dustless mind, a mind of great majesty and virtue, a good mind, a vast mind, an unequaled mind, a most profound mind, a mind that loves the Dharma, a mind that delights in the Dharma, a mind of good intent, a mind that renounces all clinging, a mind that cuts off the afflictions of all beings, a mind that closes every evil destiny.

They walk in the course of wisdom, and have already perfected immeasurable merit. In the factors of concentration and enlightenment they can expound well. Ever sporting in utmost bodhi, they diligently cultivate and proclaim it. The fleshly eye is opened and can discern and choose. The divine eye appears and beholds all Buddha-lands. The Dharma eye is pure and can be free of all attachment. The wisdom eye penetrates and reaches the farther shore. The Buddha eye is perfected, awakening and revealing. They give rise to unobstructed wisdom and broadly expound it for others. Within the three realms they cultivate equally and diligently. Having tamed themselves, they can also tame all sentient beings. They can cause others to attain supreme śamatha. In all dharmas they realize that nothing is attained. They can expound the Dharma well, with words ingenious and skillful. They diligently make offering to all Buddhas. They crush and subdue all the afflictions of sentient beings. They are pleasing to the Tathāgatas, and can be thus. Thinking thus, when they think thus, they can gather and see that all dharmas are unattained. By skillful wisdom they cultivate the dharma of cessation. They well know what to take and what to relinquish, and the sense of what accords with principle and what does not. In both the sense that accords with principle and the sense that does not, they are wholly skillful. In worldly speech their minds take no delight. In the scriptures that transcend the world they are faithful and diligent. They skillfully seek out all dharmas. Seeking all dharmas, they increase their understanding. They know that dharmas are originally without substance and cannot be grasped, and in the place they walk there is neither taking nor relinquishing. Released from old age and sickness, they abide in all virtues. From the very beginning they have dwelt in spiritual penetration, and diligently cultivate the profound Dharma. In the most profound Dharma they do not turn back. In the hard-to-understand Dharma they wholly penetrate. They attain the one-vehicle path and have no doubt. In the Buddha's teaching they do not awaken by means of another. Their wisdom is vast and deep, likened to the great sea. Their bodhi is lofty and broad, compared to Mount Sumeru. Their own majestic light surpasses sun and moon. Whatever they ponder and choose accords with wisdom. Like a snowy mountain, their minds are white and pure. Their light shines everywhere, with boundless merit, burning up the firewood of affliction. Compared to fire, they are not shaken by good or evil. Their minds are still and ever at peace, like the great earth. They wash away confusion as with pure water. Their minds have no master, like fire; they cling to nothing in the world, like wind. They nourish all beings like the earth, and view all worlds as empty space. They bear living beings like a fine carriage. Unstained by worldly dharmas, they are like the lotus. They spread far the sound of Dharma like a peal of thunder. They rain down all dharmas like a great rain. Their light covers the sages and worthies like that of the great seer. They can tame and subdue like the great elephant. Valiant and fearless like the lion king. They shelter beings like the banyan tree. Unmoved by other doctrines, like the Iron Ring Mountain. Cultivating boundless loving-kindness, like the Ganges. As kings of all good dharmas they can lead the way, like Great Brahmā. Accumulating nothing, like a flying bird. Crushing other doctrines, like the golden-winged king. Hard to meet and rare, like the udumbara flower. Supreme among men, their minds are upright. Without indolence, they can cultivate well. Among all views they skillfully decide. Gentle and patient, without jealousy. Discoursing on Dharma without satiety, seeking Dharma without weariness. Ever diligently expounding, benefiting beings. Their precepts are like crystal, clear within and without. Hearing all dharmas well, they become a supreme treasure. The words they speak make the assembly rejoice and submit. By the power of wisdom they raise the great Dharma banner, blow the great Dharma conch, beat the great Dharma drum. Ever delighting in diligent cultivation, they set up the markers of Dharma. By the light of wisdom their minds are without confusion. Far from all faults, they do no harm either. With pure minds they are apart from all defilement. Ever practicing generous giving, they forever renounce stinginess and greed. By nature gentle, they ever hold shame and modesty. Their minds are still and settled, their wisdom bright and discerning. They become lamps for the world, shattering the darkness of beings. Worthy of offerings, a peerless field of merit. As great guides they bring relief to all creatures. Far from like and dislike, their minds are pure and without care. Advancing bravely without fear, they are great generals of Dharma. Knowing the hells, they tame self and other. Benefiting sentient beings, they draw out the poisoned arrows. As knowers of the world, as teachers of the world, they guide the host of beings to renounce all clinging to love. Forever free of the three defilements, they sport in spiritual penetration.

The power of cause, the power of conditions, the power of vows, the power of arousal, the power of the conventional, the power of production, the power of roots of goodness, the power of samādhi, the power of hearing, the power of renunciation, the power of precepts, the power of patience, the power of diligence, the power of concentration, the power of wisdom, the power of śamatha, the power of vipaśyanā, the power of spiritual penetration, the power of mindfulness, the power of enlightenment, the power to crush and subdue all the great armies of Māra, together with the power of the Dharma over other doctrines, the power to shatter all the afflictions that are foes, and supreme great strength.

Majesty and blessing complete, marks and excellences dignified. Wisdom, eloquence, and roots of goodness perfected. Their eyes are pure, long, and broad, loved by all. Their bodies are clean, far from arrogance. With reverent minds they serve the Buddhas. In the presence of the Buddhas they plant the roots of all goodness. They uproot pride and are free of greed, anger, and delusion. Supremely auspicious, foremost among the worthy of offerings. They dwell in the supreme realm of wisdom, blazing with the light of insight. Their minds give rise to joy, heroic and fearless. Blessing and wisdom complete, without stagnation or limit. They speak only what they have heard, revealing it to all creatures. Whatever Dharma they hear, they can understand it all. In the factors of bodhi they cultivate with valor and diligence. In emptiness, marklessness, and wishlessness they ever abide, and in the samādhis of non-arising and non-ceasing. Their practice fills the site of enlightenment, far from the realm of the two vehicles.

Ananda, I now briefly speak of the true virtues of the host of great bodhisattvas born in that Land of Ultimate Bliss; all are thus. Ananda, even if my own body were to abide in life for a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, and with unobstructed eloquence I wished to fully proclaim the true virtues of those great bodhisattvas, they could not be exhausted. Ananda, those great bodhisattvas themselves, even to the end of their lives, could not know them either.”

Then the World-Honored One told Ananda: “This is the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. You should rise from your seat, join your palms in reverence, and with all five parts of the body bow to the ground in homage to that Buddha. That Buddha's name fills the ten directions. The Buddhas of each direction, numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all together praise it, without obstruction and without cease.”

Thereupon Ananda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms facing west, bowed with all five parts of the body to the ground, and said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, I now wish to see the Land of Ultimate Bliss and the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Life, and to make offering and serve the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas and hosts of bodhisattvas, and to plant all roots of goodness.”

Then the Buddha of Immeasurable Life at once sent forth a great radiance from the palm of his hand, illumining throughout a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of lands. All the great and small mountains in those Buddha-lands — the Black Mountain, the Jewel Mountain, Mount Sumeru, Mount Meru, Great Mount Meru, Mount Mucilinda, Great Mount Mucilinda, the Iron Ring Mountain, the Great Iron Ring Mountain — together with thickets and gardens, and all the palaces of devas and humans, were all seen by the Buddha's radiance. It was like a person with pure divine eye beholding a fathom of ground and seeing all that is there. Or again, like the arising of the sun's light, whereby all things are seen. In those lands, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen all saw the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Life, like the king of Mount Sumeru, illumining all Buddha-lands. Then all the Buddha-lands were clearly revealed, as if within a fathom. Because the peerless radiance of the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Life is most pure, they saw that lofty throne, and the hosts of hearers and bodhisattvas, as when the great earth is filled and overflowing with a flood, and forests, mountains, and rivers are all submerged and no longer appear, and there is only the great water. Thus, Ananda, in that Buddha-land there are no other doctrines and no different kinds of beings, save only the great host of hearers with their light of one fathom, and those great bodhisattvas with light of a hundred thousand fathoms and more, yojana upon yojana. The radiance of that Tathāgata of Immeasurable Life, the Arhat, the Truly and Fully Enlightened, outshines all hearers and bodhisattvas, and causes all sentient beings to see. In that Land of Ultimate Bliss, the hosts of bodhisattvas, hearers, humans, and devas all beheld the Sahā world, and Śākyamuni Tathāgata surrounded by the assembly of monks, preaching the Dharma.

Then the Buddha told Bodhisattva Maitreya: “Do you see this Buddha-land, perfect in pure majesty and adorned? And do you see the springs, pools, gardens, groves, and trees in the sky? You see the great earth, and even the Heaven of Ultimate Form, adorned with scattered flowers and groves in the empty space. And there are many birds dwelling in the realm of space, giving forth all kinds of sounds like the Buddha's voice, heard throughout the world. All those birds are manifested by transformation; they are not actual animals. Do you see all this?”
Maitreya said to the Buddha: “Yes, indeed, I have seen it.”

The Buddha again told Bodhisattva Maitreya: “Do you see all these beings, having entered palaces of a hundred thousand yojanas, roaming through the sky without attachment or obstruction, going throughout all lands to make offering to the Buddhas? And do you see those sentient beings, through the portions of day and night, continuing in Buddha-recitation without cease?”
Maitreya said: “Yes, indeed, I have seen it all.”
The Buddha again said: “Do you see any difference between the Heaven of Enjoying the Conjurations of Others and the people of the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the goods they enjoy and make use of?”
Maitreya said: “I see no difference at all between them.”
The Buddha told Maitreya: “Do you see the people of the Land of Ultimate Bliss dwelling in the womb?”

Maitreya said: “World-Honored One, it is like the devas of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, or of the Yāma Heaven, entering palaces a hundred yojanas or five hundred yojanas wide and sporting there in joy. I see the people of the Land of Ultimate Bliss who dwell as in a womb as being like the Yāma devas within their palaces. And I see other beings seated cross-legged within lotus flowers, born by transformation of themselves.”
Then Bodhisattva Maitreya again said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, for what reason are the beings of that land some born from the womb and some born by transformation?”

The Buddha told Maitreya: “If there are beings who fall into doubt and regret, who heap up roots of goodness and seek the Buddha's wisdom, universal wisdom, inconceivable wisdom, unequaled wisdom, majestic wisdom, and vast wisdom, yet cannot bring forth faith in their own roots of goodness — by this cause, for five hundred years they dwell in palaces, and do not see the Buddha, do not hear the Dharma, and do not see the host of bodhisattvas and hearers. But if there are beings who cut off doubt and regret, who heap up roots of goodness and seek the Buddha's wisdom, even to vast wisdom, and who have faith in their own roots of goodness — such a person is seated cross-legged within a lotus flower, born by transformation of a sudden, and emerges in an instant, as when someone comes from another land. And these bodhisattvas are likewise so. Bodhisattvas who arouse the mind in other lands and come to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss see the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, make offering and serve him, and likewise the hosts of bodhisattvas and hearers. Ajita, you see those of peerless wisdom: because of the power of their vast insight, they receive that transformation birth, seated cross-legged within a lotus flower. You see those of lesser kind: for five hundred years they do not see the Buddha, do not hear the Dharma, do not see the host of bodhisattvas and hearers; not knowing the deportment and rules of the bodhisattvas, and unable to cultivate the merits, they have no cause to serve the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. All such people are so because of former conditions of doubt and regret. It is like a king of the kṣatriya caste whose son breaks the law. He is confined within the inner palace and placed in a flowered pavilion, with tiered towers and fair halls, wondrously adorned with rare treasures, jeweled canopies and golden couches, layered with cushions, famous flowers strewn on the ground, great precious incense burning, and all that he wears and uses richly provided. Yet with Jambu gold his two feet are bound in chains.”
The Buddha told Maitreya: “What do you think? Would the mind of that prince take delight in this?”

He answered: “No, World-Honored One. While he is confined, he ever thinks of release. He seeks out kinsmen and friends, householders, ministers, elders, and close attendants. Though the king's own son longs to get out, it never goes as he wishes. Only when the kṣatriya king's heart is gladdened does he obtain release.”

The Buddha told Maitreya: “So it is, so it is. If there are those who fall into doubt and regret, who plant roots of goodness and seek the Buddha's wisdom, even to vast wisdom, yet cannot bring forth faith in their own roots of goodness — because they have heard the Buddha's name and given rise to a mind of faith, though they are born in that land, they cannot emerge from within the lotus. Those beings dwell in the flower-womb, with the thought that it is a garden or a palace. Why? Because within it all is pure, without any filth or evil, and there is nothing whatever that is displeasing. Yet those beings, for five hundred years, do not see the Buddha, do not hear the Dharma, do not see the bodhisattvas and the host of hearers, and cannot make offering or serve the Buddhas. They cannot ask about the bodhisattvas' treasury of Dharma, and are far from all peerless roots of goodness. In that state they give rise to no delight, and cannot emerge to cultivate good dharmas. Only when the faults of former lives are wholly exhausted do they then come forth. And when they come forth, their minds are confused as to above and below and the four directions. If for five hundred years they are free of doubt, they will make offering to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas, and plant immeasurable and boundless roots of goodness. You, Ajita, should know that doubt brings great harm to bodhisattvas.”
Then Bodhisattva Maitreya said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, within this land, how many are the bodhisattvas of non-retrogression who shall be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss?”

The Buddha told Maitreya: “In this Buddha-land there are seventy-two koṭis of bodhisattvas who, in the presence of immeasurable koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, have planted roots of goodness, achieved non-retrogression, and shall be born in that land. How much more so the other bodhisattvas who, by lesser roots of goodness, are born in that land — they cannot be counted. Ajita, from the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata Patience-Enduring there are eighteen koṭis of non-retrogressing bodhisattvas who shall be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. In the Buddha-land of Precious Treasury in the northeast there are ninety koṭis of non-retrogressing bodhisattvas who shall be born in that land. From the land of the Tathāgata Immeasurable Sound there are twenty-two koṭis of non-retrogressing bodhisattvas who shall be born in that land. From the land of the Tathāgata Light there are thirty-two koṭis of non-retrogressing bodhisattvas who shall be born in that land. From the land of the Tathāgata Dragon Deva there are fourteen koṭis of non-retrogressing bodhisattvas who shall be born in that land. From the land of the Tathāgata Supreme Heavenly Power there are twelve thousand non-retrogressing bodhisattvas who shall be born in that land. From the land of the Tathāgata Lion there are five hundred non-retrogressing bodhisattvas who shall be born in that land. From the land of the Tathāgata Free of Dust there are eighty-one koṭis of non-retrogressing bodhisattvas who shall be born in that land. From the land of the Tathāgata World Deva there are sixty koṭis of non-retrogressing bodhisattvas who shall be born in that land. From the land of the Tathāgata Supreme Accumulation there are sixty koṭis of non-retrogressing bodhisattvas who shall be born in that land. From the land of the Tathāgata King of Humans there are ten koṭis of non-retrogressing bodhisattvas who shall be born in that land. From the land of the Tathāgata Supreme Flower there are five hundred bodhisattvas, perfect in great diligence, who have set their course upon the one vehicle and can, within seven days, free beings from the round of birth and death through a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of kalpas; they too shall be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. From the land of the Tathāgata Arousing Diligence there are sixty-nine koṭis of non-retrogressing bodhisattvas who shall be born in that land. Having reached that land, they make offering and pay homage to the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Life and the host of bodhisattvas.

Ajita, were I to speak fully of the bodhisattvas of all directions born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss — those already arrived, now arriving, and yet to arrive, who make offering, pay homage, and gaze in reverence upon the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and others — to tell only their names would not be exhausted in a whole kalpa. Ajita, you see how those great bodhisattvas have well gained benefit. If there are those who hear the name of that Buddha and can give rise to a single thought of joyful love, they shall obtain the merit spoken of above. Their minds are neither base nor arrogant. The roots of goodness they perfect are all increased. Ajita, therefore I tell you, and the devas, humans, asuras, and the rest of the world: this Dharma gate I now entrust to you. You should love and delight in cultivating it, and even for a single day and night receive, uphold, read, and recite it, giving rise to a mind of hope. In the great assembly, reveal it for others. You should cause it to be written out and to hold the scrolls of the sutra. Within this sutra, give rise to the thought of a guiding teacher. Ajita, therefore, bodhisattvas who wish to cause immeasurable hosts of beings swiftly to abide in non-retrogression upon utmost, perfect bodhi, and who wish to see that vast adornment, and to receive the perfect merit of peerless Buddha-lands, should rouse the power of diligence and listen to this Dharma gate. Even should they pass through a billion worlds filled with raging fire, for the sake of seeking the Dharma they should not give rise to a mind of retreat, crookedness, or deceit. Read, recite, receive, and uphold it; write out the scrolls of the sutra. Even for a single moment, reveal it for others. Exhort them to listen, and let them not give rise to grief. Though they enter a great fire, they should not doubt or regret. Why? Because those immeasurable koṭis of bodhisattvas all seek this subtle and wondrous Dharma gate, revere and listen to it, and give rise to no opposition. Therefore you should seek this Dharma.

Ajita, those beings gain great benefit. If in future ages, even when the true Dharma is perishing, there are beings who plant roots of goodness, who have already made offering to immeasurable Buddhas — by the added power of those Tathāgatas they can obtain this vast Dharma gate. All Tathāgatas praise and approve it. If one grasps and upholds that Dharma, one shall obtain the vast wisdom of all wisdom. As one's heart delights, one plants all roots of goodness. If good men and good women have great and peerless resolve in that Dharma, they can hear it and obtain great joy. Receive, uphold, read, and recite it, broadly expound it for others, and ever delight in cultivating it.

Ajita, immeasurable koṭis in number of bodhisattvas and the rest have sought and requested this Dharma and have never turned from it in weariness. Therefore you, good men and good women, in this present and in future lives, if you have sought, now seek, or shall seek this Dharma, shall all obtain good benefit. Ajita, what the Tathāgata ought to do he has done. You should abide without doubt and plant roots of goodness. You should ever study and cultivate, so that you have no doubt or stagnation and do not enter the prisons fashioned of all kinds of precious treasures. Ajita, such great ones of majesty and virtue can bring forth the vast and varied gates of the Buddha Dharma.

Because this Dharma is not heard, one koṭi of bodhisattvas have turned back from utmost, perfect bodhi. Ajita, the appearance of a Buddha in the world is rare, and a body free of the eight difficulties is also hard to obtain. The unsurpassed Dharma of the Tathāgatas — the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the unobstructed and unattached, the most profound Dharma, and the bodhisattvas' Dharma of the pāramitās — is also hard for one who can speak the Dharma to reveal. Ajita, one who speaks the Dharma well is not easily met. Firm and deep faith is likewise hard to encounter in its time. Therefore I now proclaim it in accordance with principle, and you should cultivate and abide as taught. You, Ajita, I entrust with this Dharma gate and with the Dharma of the Buddhas. You should practice it and not let it perish. Such a vast, subtle, and wondrous Dharma gate is praised by all Buddhas. Do not disobey the Buddha's teaching and cast it away, lest you obtain unlucky benefit, sink into the long night, and be filled with every peril and suffering. Therefore I now make this great entrustment, that this Dharma may long abide and not perish. You should diligently cultivate and accord with my teaching. Then the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
If in merit one has never yet cultivated, one never hears this subtle Dharma.
The valiant who accomplish every good shall hear a sutra thus profound.
That one has seen the World-Honored Ones, who shed great light to save a turbid age.
Much-hearing, retentive as the mighty sea, that one wins the love of sages and worthies.
The indolent, the wrong-viewed, the base, do not believe the Tathāgata's true Dharma.
But one who once planted goodness in the Buddhas can cultivate the work that saves the world.
As the blind, forever in the dark, cannot guide another on the road,
so too the hearers as to Buddha-wisdom; how much less other beings can comprehend it.
The Tathāgata's merit the Buddha alone knows; only the World-Honored One can reveal it.
Devas, dragons, and yakṣas cannot reach it; the two vehicles are themselves cut off from words.
If all beings are to become Buddhas, their course surpasses Samantabhadra and reaches the farther shore.
To expound the merit of one Buddha would take inconceivable kalpas of time.
Though in the midst of it his body should pass into cessation, the Buddha's peerless wisdom cannot be measured.
Therefore, being complete in faith and hearing, and taken in hand by good friends,
one may hear so profound and wondrous a Dharma, and shall win the love of all the holy ones.
The Tathāgata's peerless wisdom fills all space; the words he speaks the Buddha alone awakens to.
Therefore you learned ones of broad hearing should believe my teaching as words of truth.
A human body is very hard to gain, and a Buddha's appearance in the world is hard to meet.
Faith and wisdom are won only after long time; therefore the cultivator should be diligent.
Having heard this wondrous Dharma, ever recollect the Buddhas and give rise to joy.
That one was in past times truly my friend, and can well delight in and desire the Buddha's bodhi.

Then, when the World-Honored One had spoken this sutra, among devas and humans there were twelve thousand nayutas of koṭis of beings who, far from dust and defilement, obtained the pure Dharma eye. Twenty koṭis of beings obtained the fruit of the non-returner. Six thousand eight hundred monks, their outflows exhausted, attained liberation of mind. Forty koṭis of bodhisattvas abided in non-retrogression upon utmost bodhi, donned the great armor, and shall attain true enlightenment. There were twenty-five koṭis of beings who attained the patience of non-retrogression. There were four myriads of koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of beings who had never before aroused the thought of utmost bodhi but now for the first time aroused it, planted all roots of goodness, vowed to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and to see Amitabha Buddha; all shall be born in that Tathāgata's land, and each in a different region shall in turn become a Buddha, all bearing the same name, Wondrous Sound. There were eight myriads of koṭis of nayutas of beings who attained the Dharma-patience of prediction and shall accomplish utmost bodhi. Those whom the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, when he formerly walked the bodhisattva path, brought to maturity, shall all be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and their former vows and aspirations, remembered and fulfilled, shall all be accomplished.

Then in the billion worlds there were six kinds of quaking, and all manner of rare and wondrous transformations appeared, and a great radiance was sent forth, illumining the whole world. Immeasurable koṭis of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of devas and humans at once made music that sounded of itself without being struck. Celestial māndārava flowers rained down, covering the ground to the knee, and even in the Heaven of Ultimate Form all manner of peerless and wondrous offerings were made.

When the Buddha had finished speaking the sutra, Bodhisattva Maitreya and the rest, together with the venerable Ananda and the whole great assembly, hearing what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly joyful.

blocks.text: The Sutra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment

inline.s: Translated by imperial command by the Tripiṭaka master of the Western Heavens, the court gentleman for consultation, the acting director of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, the Great Master of Illustrious Teaching, the minister Fǎxián.

Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was in the city of Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak, together with a great assembly of thirty-two thousand great monks. All had attained arhatship and possessed great spiritual penetration. Their names were: the venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the venerable Aśvajit, the venerable
li
he
zun

na, the venerable Maitrāyaṇīputra, the venerable Aniruddha, the venerable Nanda, the venerable Kiṃbhila, the venerable Subhūti, the venerable Revata, the venerable Kharadeva, the venerable Mahārevata, the venerable Pārāyaṇika, the venerable Vakkula, the venerable Ānanda, the venerable Rāhula, the venerable Svāgata. Thus were they, thirty-two thousand in all.

Then the venerable Ananda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms and bowed in reverence, and said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Truly and Fully Enlightened, has pure faculties and a perfect countenance, and his Buddha-land is adorned. Such merit as this has never been. What is the course he has walked, the vast and wondrous course, and the course walked by the Buddhas of past and future? May you proclaim it for us.”

The Buddha told Ananda: “Excellent, excellent. For the benefit of all beings, bearing a mind of compassion and pity, you can ask the Tathāgata about this subtle meaning. Listen well now, and ponder it well. The Tathāgata, the Worthy of Offerings, the Truly and Fully Enlightened, will now speak it for you.

The Buddha told Ananda: “As in the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a World-Honored Buddha who appeared in the world, named the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, the Arhat, the Truly and Fully Enlightened. Before that Dīpaṃkara Buddha there was again a World-Honored One who appeared in the world, named the Tathāgata Pradīpaśikhin. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Light-Sender. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Caṇḍanagandha-protecting Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Sumeru Kalpa Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Moon Face Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Stainless Face Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Unattached Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Dragon Lord Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Sun Face Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named King of Mountain-Echo Sound Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Sumeru Peak Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Golden Treasury Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Fire Light Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Immovable Ground Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Crystal Light Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Moon King Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Sun Sound Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Scattered Flower Adornment Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Auspicious Peak Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named King of Ocean-Upholding Wisdom, Mastery, and Penetration Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Light-Giver Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Great Fragrant Elephant Light Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Free of All Stain Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Valiant Peak Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Jewel Light Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Upholder of Many Virtues and Attainer of Penetration Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Surpassing Sun and Moon Light Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Supreme Crystal Light Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Wisdom-Flower Unfolding, Mind-Course Born Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named King of the Great Flower Grove of Penetration Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named One Moon Light Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Shatterer of Ignorance and Darkness Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named Canopy of Pearl and Coral Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named King of the Self-Mastery of the Three Vehicles Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named King of the Self-Mastery of the Lion Ocean Peak Tathāgata. And before that Buddha there was a Buddha named King of the Self-Mastery of the Brahma Voice Tathāgata.

And before that Buddha there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja, the Arhat, the Truly and Fully Enlightened, the Perfect in Wisdom and Conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Devas and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. And within his Dharma there was a monk named Dharmākara. He was first in faith and understanding, first in clear memory, first in cultivation, first in diligence, first in wisdom, first in the Great Vehicle. Then that monk left his own place and came before the Buddha. He bowed his head to the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and straightway praised the Buddha in verse for the dignity of his countenance. Then he again brought forth vast and great vows, saying in verse:
The Tathāgata's subtle countenance, majestic and fair, has no equal in all the world.
His boundless light illumines the ten directions; sun, moon, fire, and pearls all hide their brightness.
May I attain the Buddha's pure voice, whose Dharma sound spreads without bound.
Proclaiming the gate of precepts, concentration, and diligence, penetrating the profound and wondrous Dharma.
Wisdom vast and deep as the sea, the mind within pure, cut off from the toil of dust.
Transcending the boundless gates of evil destiny, swiftly reaching the ultimate shore of bodhi.
Like the immeasurable Buddhas of the past, whose majestic light shines over all realms of beings.
As a great guide for that host of beings, ferrying them from old age and death to peace.
Ever practicing giving, precepts, and patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom — the six pāramitās.
May the beings not yet ferried be ferried, and those already ferried be brought to Buddhahood.
With all things I make offering, a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas.
To the Buddha-World-Honored Ones, countless as the sands of the Ganges, may I accomplish the fruit of cessation.
And there are Buddha-lands in the ten directions that ever send forth light illumining all.
With peerless adornment beyond all compare, may I accomplish the benefit of the host of beings.
In all the worlds without bound, and the kinds of beings that turn through the destinies.
May they swiftly be born in my land and receive joy, and before long all attain the unsurpassed Way.
May I be ever diligent and firm in resolve, ever moving a compassionate mind to draw out beings.
Until the suffering beings of the Avīci hell are all ferried, my vast vows shall never cease.

Then the World-Honored One told Ananda: “When that monk Dharmākara had spoken these verses, he said to the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja: ‘I now arouse the mind of utmost, perfect bodhi, and delight in seeking the unsurpassed, true, and equal enlightenment. May the World-Honored One speak of the merit and adornment of the Buddhas' lands. If I may hear it, I shall ever cultivate and uphold the practice of adorning a land.’”
Then the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja told the monk Dharmākara: “Ponder for yourself what skillful means you would cultivate to accomplish the adornment of a Buddha-land?”

The monk said: “My wisdom is shallow and slight; I cannot know the practice of adorning a land. The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Truly and Fully Enlightened, may proclaim for me the matter of the adornment of the Buddhas' lands.”

Then the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja straightway proclaimed for him the marks of the vast, perfect merit and adornment of eighty-four hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-lands. Only after a whole kalpa could it be brought to an end.”
Then Ananda, having heard this, said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, how long was the life of that Buddha Lokeśvararāja, that he could speak of lands for a whole kalpa?”

The Buddha told Ananda: “That Buddha's life was fully forty kalpas. Ananda, when that monk Dharmākara heard the Buddha speak of the merit and adornment of eighty-four hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, he understood and penetrated it all as clearly as a single Buddha-land. Then in that assembly he bowed his head to the Buddha's feet, took leave of the Buddha and withdrew, and went to a quiet place, where he sat alone in contemplation, cultivating merit and adorning a Buddha-land. He brought forth great vows and passed five kalpas. Then the monk Dharmākara again came to where the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja was. He bowed with all five parts of the body to the ground in homage to the World-Honored One's feet. Having bowed, he joined his palms and said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, the merit and adornment of those eighty-four hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, and the practices and vows thereof, I have now accomplished.”

Then the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja told the monk: “Excellent, excellent. Your practice and vows are pondered to the utmost. Now is the very time: expound them for the assembly. Then the bodhisattvas, hearing this Dharma, will obtain great benefit and can cultivate the adornment of Buddha-lands.”
Then the monk Dharmākara, hearing the Buddha's holy command, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and straightway proclaimed:

World-Honored One, I make this vow: may I, like the World-Honored One, realize utmost, perfect bodhi; and may the Buddha-land in which I dwell be perfect in immeasurable, inconceivable merit and adornment. May all beings, and all in the realm of Yama, in the three evil paths — hells, hungry ghosts, and animals — be born in my land and receive the transformation of my Dharma. Before long they shall all accomplish utmost, perfect bodhi, and all shall obtain bodies of true golden color.

World-Honored One, when I have attained bodhi and accomplished true enlightenment, may all beings in the worlds of the ten directions who are born in my land be as in the lands of the Buddhas, among the hosts of humans and devas. Far from discrimination, their faculties stilled, may they all be made to attain utmost, perfect bodhi.

World-Honored One, when I have attained bodhi and accomplished true enlightenment, may all beings in the worlds of the ten directions who are born in my land obtain great spiritual penetration. In a single thought they shall travel throughout and visit a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, make offering to the Buddhas, and deeply plant roots of goodness, and all shall be made to attain utmost, perfect bodhi.

World-Honored One, when I have attained bodhi and accomplished true enlightenment, may all beings born in my land all obtain the penetration of past lives, and be able well to observe the matters of past kalpas, a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of them, and all shall be made to attain utmost, perfect bodhi.

World-Honored One, when I have attained bodhi and accomplished true enlightenment, may all beings born in my land all obtain the pure divine eye, and be able to see the coarse and fine marks of a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of worlds, and all shall be made to attain utmost, perfect bodhi.

World-Honored One, when I have attained bodhi and accomplished true enlightenment, may all beings born in my land all obtain the penetration of others' minds, and be able well to know the minds and mental factors of a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of beings, and all shall be made to attain utmost, perfect bodhi.

World-Honored One, when I have attained bodhi and accomplished true enlightenment, may all beings born in my land all abide in the stage of right faith, be free of inverted thought, and cultivate firmly, and all shall be made to attain utmost, perfect bodhi.

World-Honored One, when I have attained bodhi and accomplished true enlightenment, may all beings born in my land have immeasurable roots of goodness from the right practices they cultivate, pervading the realm of perfect stillness without interruption, and all shall be made to attain utmost, perfect bodhi.

World-Honored One, when I have attained bodhi and accomplished true enlightenment, may all beings born in my land, though they abide in the stages of hearers and solitary realizers, go within a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of jeweled lands and perform the Buddha's work everywhere, and all shall be made to attain utmost, perfect bodhi.

World-Honored One, when I have attained bodhi and accomplished true enlightenment, may all beings born in my land all obtain boundless light, and be able to illumine a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas' lands, and all shall be made to attain utmost, perfect bodhi.
